name: Femi Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Femi. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government, and what you say is confidential. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do parcel drops in the daytime for Packwise, which is an app, in my late dad's old Astra estate, about 110 drops on a good day. Then from six I do takeaway orders on ChopChop until about ten, mostly pizzas and curries around the town. On Sundays I don't work at all, that's church and lunch at my mum's.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What matters most to you outside work right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Ruth, my fiancée, and the wedding next August at St Michael's. Ruth works at a children's nursery, and we're saving for the wedding and a deposit, but honestly the savings are small, less than a month's bills. Everything I do now is about getting married properly and not starting on debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, a lot of noise about nothing. Hard work still counts, same as it did for my dad. I'd say that after church to the men at coffee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep going and keep saving, and the wedding is still the big pressure. Packwise, the parcel app, dropped the rate twice this year, so I'm working more hours for the same money, and the wedding's next August. If the Astra goes, we've got nothing to replace it with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep both apps going, six days a week, no Sundays. I'd cut the wedding guest list from 120 to 80, which Ruth already suggested. And I'd ask my uncle Tunde, who has a tiling business, if he needs a hand on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, but at peace with it. I know what I'm working for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why no Sundays, even when money is tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my dad never worked Sundays, and he drove a bus for 30 years. It's the one day I'm a person and not a driver. I'd rather work later on Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you make of the apps cutting rates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's business, they're allowed. If I don't like it, I should find better work, and that's on me. I don't want the government telling them what to pay, that just makes everything cost more.

say: AI was **noise about nothing**, and hard work still counts.
He'd say it after church to **the men at coffee**.
think: The **wedding** next August is the big pressure, with savings under a month.
Packwise has **cut the parcel rate** twice this year, so he works longer.
do: Keep **both apps** going six days a week, never Sundays.
Cut the **wedding guest list** from 120 to 80.
Ask his **uncle Tunde** for Saturday tiling work.
feel: **Tired** but at peace, because he knows what he's working for.
S0.quote: Packwise, the parcel app, dropped the rate twice this year, so I'm working more hours for the same money, and the wedding's next August.
fieldNote: Femi's pressure is his **wedding** and two app rate cuts, not technology.
He accepts rate cuts as **just business** and opposes the state setting pay.
His **Sunday rule** comes from his late father and he won't break it for money.

steps.text: Keep driving Packwise days and ChopChop evenings, six days a week
Cut the wedding guest list from 120 to 80
Ask uncle Tunde for Saturday labouring on his tiling jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to get on with it and not wait for handouts. Learn a trade, work hard. I'd say that at church and to anyone who complained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry about all the office lads who lose work and start on ChopChop. Less orders for me, and they've got newer cars. I'm not learning any AI, I barely trust the app I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Uncle Tunde properly for an apprenticeship in tiling, starting part-time. I'd keep driving to pay for the wedding. And I'd ask the pastor if the church knows anyone hiring, because the church looks after its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like there's a storm coming but nobody's said the date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not learning AI. If tiling firms start using it for quotes, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncle Tunde would do the quotes, not me. I'd be on my knees with the trowel. If it ever came to it, I'd ask Ruth to show me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You told others to learn a trade. Would you say the same to yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point, yes. Learn a trade, work hard, I tell people at church, and honestly I'm talking about me as much as anyone. I've been putting it off for three years.

say: People should get on with it and **not wait for handouts**.
**Learn a trade** and work hard, he'd tell church friends.
think: Laid-off office workers on ChopChop would mean **fewer orders** for him.

Keep **driving** to pay for the wedding.
Ask the **pastor** whether anyone in church is hiring.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a storm coming with no date set.
S1.quote: Learn a trade, work hard, I tell people at church, and honestly I'm talking about me as much as anyone.
fieldNote: Femi admits he's been **putting off** a trade for three years.
He expects **competition** from laid-off office workers on the food app.
He leans on **church and family**, not the state, for help finding work.

steps.text: Start part-time tiling apprenticeship with uncle Tunde
Keep both delivery apps going to fund the wedding
Ask the pastor at St Michael's about anyone hiring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after families and churches, because those are what hold people up when things fall apart. I wouldn't say the government should pay everyone, that's not right either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared. AI in 2028 doesn't touch my driving, but the robots in 2031 would. I'd be 32, newly married, maybe a baby on the way, and no trade when the delivery robots come in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start tiling with Uncle Tunde full-time as soon as he'd have me, even for less money. We'd push the wedding back a year, or do it small at the church hall. I'd keep the Astra running for ChopChop evenings while I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared for Ruth, honestly, more than me. I said I'd look after her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would tiling be safe from robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old bathrooms, wonky walls, I can't see a robot doing that by 2031. But I don't really know. Maybe it's just what I want to believe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell Ruth you want to delay the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd probably say it before I could. She's more sensible than me. Her mum would be upset, though, she's already bought a hat.

say: **Families and churches** must hold people up when things fall apart.
The government **shouldn't pay everyone**, he'd say.
think: Robots arriving around **2031** would end his driving at 32.
He'd be newly married, maybe with a **baby**, and no trade.
do: Start tiling with his uncle **full-time**, even for less money.
**Push the wedding** back a year or hold it small in the church hall.
Keep the **Astra** running for ChopChop evenings while he learns.
feel: **Scared for Ruth** more than himself, because he promised to look after her.
S2.quote: I'd be 32, newly married, maybe a baby on the way, and no trade when the delivery robots come in 2031.
fieldNote: Femi feels **responsible** for his fiancée Ruth, which drives his alarm.
He admits tiling's safety may be **wishful thinking**.
Delaying the wedding is a **real cost**: his future mother-in-law has already bought a hat.

steps.text: Join uncle Tunde's tiling business full-time on lower pay
Push the St Michael's wedding back a year
Keep ChopChop evening shifts in the Astra while training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for any man to learn a trade if he's willing. I'd say that at church, and mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for AI and eight for robots gives me till about 2034 driving. I'd get married on time, do the tiling apprenticeship properly, and be a tiler before the robots come for my car. It's still a race, but I can see the finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the wedding date and go small. I'd start with Uncle Tunde on Saturdays this year, then two days a week next year. By 2029 I'd want to be tiling full-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better, but still nervous. Like a long drive at night, you know where you're going but you can't see far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your church friends who also drive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi drives for Packwise too, so I'd tell him to come tile with me. Or find his own trade. Nobody's coming to save delivery drivers like us, so we save ourselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you feel about the robots, deep down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't like it. Something's lost when people stop working with their hands. But it's not my place to stop progress, I just have to make my way.

He'd say it at **church** and mean it.
think: He'd have until about **2034** driving, enough time to become a tiler.

do: Keep the **wedding date** and hold a small wedding.
Tile with his uncle on **Saturdays** this year, then two days next year.
feel: **Nervous**, like a long night drive where you can't see far ahead.
S3.quote: Nobody's coming to save delivery drivers like us, so we save ourselves.
fieldNote: Femi would keep his **wedding** date because five years allows it.
He dislikes robots in principle but **won't oppose progress**, fitting his free-market views.

steps.text: Hold a small wedding at St Michael's on the planned date
Tile with uncle Tunde on Saturdays, then two weekdays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, people have no excuse. Work hard and prepare, same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years for AI and thirteen for robots, so maybe 2039 before a robot takes my seat in my dad's old Astra. That's a whole life, wedding, kids, maybe a house. I'd still want a trade, but I wouldn't panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get married next August as planned. I'd do the tiling on Saturdays for a couple of years and see if I like it. I'd try to save for a deposit, maybe £100 a month at first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, mostly. The usual worry about money, but I can live with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd see if you like tiling. What if you don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd look at something else, maybe bus driving like my dad. But robots would get buses too, wouldn't they. I'd still have to find something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years make you put things off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might, honestly. That's my weakness, Ruth says. I'd need her pushing me.

say: Ten years is a **long time**, so people have no excuse.
Work hard and **prepare**, he'd say, same as always.
think: Robots might take his seat around **2039**, after wedding, kids and maybe a house.
He'd still want a **trade**, but without panic.
do: Try **Saturday tiling** for a couple of years to see if he likes it.
Save **£100 a month** toward a house deposit.
S4.quote: Ten years for AI and thirteen for robots, so maybe 2039 before a robot takes my seat in my dad's old Astra.
fieldNote: Femi's **wedding stays on track** with ten years of warning.
His remaining worry is **money**, not AI, so he stays anxious.

steps.text: Marry Ruth next August as planned
Try Saturday tiling with uncle Tunde for two years
Save £100 a month toward a house deposit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be newly married with no trade and only three years. What would help is real apprenticeships, paid properly, so a man can learn a trade and still feed his family. Not handouts, just a fair start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. When everything changes, people need something that doesn't. St Michael's church has been standing for 200 years, and it'll be standing after the robots.

headlineQuote: St Michael's church has been standing for 200 years, and it'll be standing after the robots.
portrait: Femi is **27**, drives his late father's Astra for two delivery apps and never works Sundays.
He's **engaged** to Ruth, a nursery worker, with a wedding planned for next August.
He trusts **family and church** over government and refuses to use AI tools.
In every AGI picture he turns to **tiling** with his uncle; the time available decides the wedding date.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be newly married with no trade and three years.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** so a man can learn a trade and feed his family.
